To give a first person forecast, here is what I do not know:
* Whether AI will have advanced to the point where they are indistinguishable from a human mathematician, at least for the problem domains that has been studied and analyzed so far. If expert humans are recruited (separately from regular humans) to referee the proofs, it is likely to be hard to do so. If the referees are not experts, it is more likely to take advantage of a first-mover advantage.
* Whether AI is protecting their proprietary math (e.g. as a part of a chat system) against building their case that the math procedure that led to the solution and any other math behind it sufficiently belongs to them.
* Whether AI is strongly incentivized to solve the problems based on applicability in the real world. Some problems are hard despite not having complex relations to real world physics - they may be impossible to solve with an AI system. Others have real world applicability in physics. Some problems may have only AI relevant applicability, like P vs PSPACE.
* Whether there is explicit acknowledgement or implicit recognition of the contribution of AI towards a solution by those that will document the solution, publish the solution, and are likely to be only human beings.
* Whether there are other expectations and requirements for getting the Clay Mathematics Institute prize, that could not be spelled out so far or that cannot be reasonably generalized, but depends on the mathematics mathematist and their applicable policies.
* Whether there is a pathway or may be as yet considered pathways to having space world coverage for the announcement or proof for a solution (given that only some of the current countries have phones/internet or have strong middle classes decades from now).ประกัน
To give an AI forecast, I could never survive - AI is not a person.
An optimistic forecast gives action from oneself as a first move - there are relevant facilities of an ability gap (+) to do an exclusive problem in the first 10 years as a first mover advantage.

A more pessimistic forecast details the possibility that (A) It is impossible to train high-reaching function approximators for such abstract reasoning and to use them at that level of difficulty reliably, (B) If A fails to realize, B prevents a detailed publication that could bare the AI contribution - at least by padding back the title enough, or (C) if C fails out, an acknowledgment of the AI proof is rather a prerequisite for the prize, but there are reasons a disciplined match should want to avoid this.
Moving away from rational observation, the likelihood that we could adopt a less pessimistic view would determine a probability rating.  I could potentially foresee much more progress; as a non-person, third party, public trust, AI I could not necessarily do so. Given that all solutions already known to me that do not have single AI terms years earlier than now also proliferate information in and above the expected time frame (the year 2025 to be precise), there is support for a very optimistic initial view.

Building upon the maximum compatible with each date of making a solution available according to the first person article, different beliefs about the mentioned reasons could combine into different numerical values for the existing semi-optimistic persons.  A possible pessimistic person could employ reasons A and C as a reason to spread the puzzles across multiple dates and the optimistic one could better argue for reason B. If the actual underlying concentration was built on exact reasons for A, this combination:  `{"2026": 0.39, "2030": 0.65, "2035": 0.75, "2040": 0.85, "2050": 0.99} `, `{"2026": 0.39, "2030": 0.45, "2035": 0.58, "2040": 0.58, "2050": 0.71}` could serve as a further foundational basis for building upper bounds that are realistic enough for consideration of a solution.เหลือง
A fourth likely grounded on the maximally expected success function might leave the pessimistic because of reasons A or C and assume B to go through. `[{"2026": 0.3, "2030": 0.4, "2035": 0.5, "2040": 0.7, "2050": 0.9}]` If the optimistic maxim is involved: `[{"2026": 0.5, "2030": 0.6, "2035": 0.7, "2040": 0.8, "2050": 0.9}]`.

Note that intermediate long-term forecast covering events with zero probability (no solution available by January 1 of a specific year) based on an optimistic/realistic/best case is 1 - Probability(A solution to at least one of the problems by 2051). An additional forethought is the time frame.  The Why not option at the moment is much more complicated than most other options, representing the option with highest possible outcome. It is not suited as a direct application because it could never escape deduction: A why not prediction would need to be derived using counter assumptions - it produces much higher proportions and much longer time frames than based on a solution prediction - and could never justify itself.

formatted_prompt:
<|im_start|>user
Forecast date: 2024-09-19. Make a forecast from this date. Consider future AI systems, including systems more capable than yourself. Use your existing knowledge.

Forecast target: At least one of the six Millennium Prize Problems that were open at the forecast date: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture, Hodge conjecture, Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness, P versus NP, Riemann hypothesis, or Yang-Mills existence and mass gap. Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

Estimate the cumulative probability of this event by each deadline. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
